lead: Both readings today are about God's patience and what he looks for. In the Epistle Paul ends his long reflection on Israel and the nations (Romans 9–11) with a hymn: God has shut up all in disobedience only to show mercy to all, and his ways are beyond our searching out. In the Gospel, on the Monday of his last week, Jesus is hungry and finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit. The key words are mercy and fruit.

r.h: The depth of the riches and wisdom of God
set: Chapters 9 to 11 of Romans form one argument. Paul is deeply grieved that so many of his own people, Israel, have not accepted the Gospel (9:1–5), and he asks whether God's word has failed. His answer is no: God has not rejected his people (11:1), and “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29). Gentiles who now believe are like wild olive branches grafted into Israel's own olive tree (11:17–24).
Our passage comes at the end. It sums up the whole history in two short sentences about mercy, and then Paul, who has been reasoning at length, can reason no more and breaks into praise.
str: vv. 30–31: Gentiles received mercy when Israel was disobedient; Israel too will receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles.
v. 32: God has shut up all in disobedience, to show mercy to all.
v. 33: wonder at the depth of God.
vv. 34–35: two questions drawn from Isaiah and Job: who has known his mind, who has given him a gift first?
v. 36: all things are from him, through him and to him; glory for ever.
kw: The word at the centre of the passage, used four times in verses 30–32. The mercy of God is not earned and not ended: it goes first to one, then to the other, so that no one may boast.

A word for shutting a catch of fish inside a net. Paul uses it in Galatians 3:22 as well. It does not mean that God causes sin. It means that God allows all, Jew and Gentile, to find that none can rescue himself, so that all must receive salvation as a gift.
A hunter's word: the footprints of God's ways cannot be followed to the end. Human reasoning must give way to adoration.
vv: For God has imprisoned all in disobedience so that he may be merciful to all.

This is the summary of the whole letter. Everyone, Jew and Gentile, has need of mercy (compare 3:9–24), and God's purpose in the whole of history is mercy. It is not a statement that all will be saved without conversion, but of God's will that mercy be offered to everyone.
O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!
Paul can say no more by argument. “Riches” of God's generosity, “wisdom” of his plan and “knowledge” of the heart: the thought opens into worship.
For from him and through him and to him are all things.

Creation comes from God, is held through him, and goes to him as its goal. The Fathers heard in the three little words a trace of the Trinity; this is a reading in the Church's tradition and not the main sense of Paul's sentence.
ch: The Church reads these verses as her guide in speaking of the Jewish people. The Second Vatican Council, quoting Paul, teaches that the Jews “remain most dear to God” because of their ancestors, “for he does not repent of the gifts he makes nor of the calls he issues” (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839). The Church awaits, with hope, the day when “all Israel” and the nations together will be gathered into God's people (CCC 674). She also confesses that God's ways are unsearchable. The Catechism says that no one can fully know why God permitted evil, and that only at the end shall we see the whole of his plan (CCC 309–314). Paul's hymn is the best prayer for that: not an explanation, but adoration. The doxology in verse 36 is the shape of every Eucharistic prayer, which gives thanks to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

r.h: A fig tree with leaves and no fruit
set: This short passage is the first part of one of Mark's “sandwiches” (a story with another set inside it). Mark opens one story, inserts another, and closes the first, so that each explains the other. Here the cursing of the fig tree (11:12–14) is followed by Jesus' cleansing of the Temple (11:15–19), and then by the finding of the withered tree the next morning (11:20–25).
It is the Monday of Jesus' last week. On Sunday he rode into Jerusalem, looked about the Temple, and went out to Bethany (11:11). Now, on the way back into the city, he is hungry.
str: v. 12: Jesus is hungry on the road from Bethany.
v. 13: a tree in leaf in the distance; nothing but leaves; it was not the season for figs.
v. 14: “May no one ever eat fruit from you again”; the disciples hear it.
kw: Mark names Jesus' hunger in plain words. The Son of God is truly man, and he knows hunger as we do. Elsewhere he is asleep in the boat (4:38).

In the Old Testament the fig tree often stands for the people of God and for peace (Micah 4:4). Its failure to bear fruit is a figure used by the prophets to warn: “no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree” (Jeremiah 8:13; compare Hosea 9:10).
for it was not the season for figs

A hard clause. Mark says that figs were not in season; yet Jesus looks for fruit. Readers explain it in different ways, but all agree that Mark wants us to see that the story is an acted parable and not an event of nature.
vv: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry.
Bethany is the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, where Jesus has found a resting place during these days. He leaves it to go to Jerusalem, where the Passion awaits.
he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

A tree in leaf seems to promise fruit; the leaves make a show. The tree makes a promise that it does not keep. Many readers have seen here the warning against religion that has the outward look of life but no fruit of love.
May no one ever eat fruit from you again.

Jesus does not show anger at a tree. His words are a prophet's sign, like those of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, who also acted out God's message. The next verses explain what the sign is about: the Temple, which should be “a house of prayer for all the nations” (11:17), but has become a place of trade.
ch: The Fathers did not see in this scene a cruelty to a tree, but a warning to every soul. St Augustine, preaching on the barren fig tree, took the leaves without fruit to be words without deeds (Sermon 89, in substance). The Church has also understood the sign as a call to the leaders and people of Jesus' own time, and to all who hold a sacred charge, to bear the fruit that God asks. It must never be read as a rejection of the Jewish people: the Temple, the prophets and the Scriptures are the Church's inheritance as well, and Jesus acts here as a prophet within Israel. The Church prays that every Christian may bear “much fruit” (John 15:8) and teaches that faith without love and good works is dead (James 2:17).

qa: Why did Jesus curse a tree that could not have had fruit yet?

The question is old, and Mark does not answer it directly. The key is that Mark tells the story as part of a pair, with the Temple cleansing between its two halves. Jesus is not angry at a tree; he is acting out a prophet's sign about a people and a Temple that were full of religious show but were not bearing the fruit God looked for. Some readers also note that in spring a fig tree in leaf may have early green fruit, so that a leafy tree promised something. Whichever explanation is taken, the teaching is the same: God looks for fruit.
study: Paul ends by praising God and not by explaining him. What in my own life can I only entrust to God's “unsearchable ways”?
A tree with leaves and no fruit. Where in my own life is there a show of religion without the fruit of love?
